response:
I strongly support reforms to increase affordable, good‑quality homes in Wales. Releasing surplus public land and capturing the planning uplift through levies or taxes would lower land costs and fund affordable housing and local infrastructure. In our area, council and NHS land sits idle while demand for affordable homes grows; if uplift from planning permission is ring-fenced for local housing and roads, parks and flood defence, it would deliver homes faster and sustain communities. For example, a derelict site near my town could provide affordable homes alongside a new primary school and cycle routes if uplift funds were earmarked locally.

Reforming Section 106, CIL and viability testing with greater transparency and enforceable obligations is essential. Publish viability assessments and set clear targets for on-site affordable homes or robust in‑lieu contributions that actually reach local housing projects and infrastructure projects. Without transparency, we risk developers paying only lip service.

Finally, require funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or prior to housing to ensure sustainable, service-ready new communities. In practice this means upfront budgets for GP capacity, school expansion and bus links, so new developments don’t overwhelm existing services.

Raising affordable, good-quality homes in my area will hinge on a careful mix of measures that stabilise rents while unlocking supply. I support pursuing targeted rent caps or stabilisation in the private rented sector, but only as part of evidence-led pilots. A local cap aligned to the average local rent (with CPI indexing and exemptions for new-builds) could stop runaway increases that push families out of area, while keeping landlords willing to invest in essential maintenance if there's predictable returns. Importantly, we should evaluate landlord exit risk and investment levels through 2-year pilots in several districts, with clear milestones on quality, vacancy rates, and new supply. Complement this with practical steps: streamline planning for conversions of vacant offices or shops into homes; small-site building incentives; and minimum energy standards plus a simple compliance route for standard upgrades to boost living conditions. In my experience as a renter, rents have risen faster than wages and maintenance times can drift; a stabilisation mechanism backed by credible evaluation could help households stay put and give builders confidence to expand supply. I support an evidence-based approach, with strong tenant protections, sunset clauses if outcomes show misalignment, and transparent publication of pilot results to inform wider rollout.

Public investment in council and housing association building is slow and misaligned with local needs; instead, prioritise streamlined planning, private delivery, and targeted grants to accelerate affordable, good-quality homes.

I welcome reforms to increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area. Key to this is better local data and robust monitoring so we can see when developer commitments are being delivered or slipping. A transparent data dashboard covering planning permissions, Section 106 obligations, delivery timetables and targets would give residents confidence and give councils the leverage to enforce deadlines. Local planning departments need sufficient capacity—more planning officers, dedicated delivery teams and clear escalation routes—so commitments aren’t quietly rolled over or watered down.

I also support more purpose-built Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management for long‑term rental supply. In practice, this means projects with long‑term occupancy management, energy efficiency standards and clearly tracked rent caps. From my experience, when a site commits to 30% affordable homes but only delivers a fraction, the housing ladder stays slanted. BTR can counter that if there are enforceable covenants and credible management.

Taken together, these reforms would help turn planning promises into genuinely affordable homes that tenants can rely on.

As a local community organisation in England, we believe reforms should place community ownership at the heart of local housing supply, alongside high quality, well managed private rental. Specifically, expand the use of community land trusts and housing cooperatives by freeing up land held by councils to be leased long term to CLTs at peppercorn rent, with robust independence from political cycles. This can shield rents from market volatility and keep homes affordable for decades. We also need to widen self build opportunities and embrace modern methods of construction such as factory built modular homes on brownfield sites; this can cut build times and raise quality, provided local planning and funding processes are predictable. On Build to Rent and mixed tenure, there is merit in schemes with affordability covenants and professional management, especially in areas with limited supply. The key is to guarantee long term affordability and transparent upkeep. In practice, this means targeted grants or loans to fund upfront land assembly, streamlined planning for community led projects, and mandatory professional on site management for BTR to avoid neglectful developments. My concern is ensuring community engagement remains central, and that governance structures prevent land from being snapped up by developers after initial subsidies. Done right, these reforms could deliver homes that are affordable and well built within a few years.

I support reforms that ensure housing is paired with funded, phased transport, schools, clinics and utilities, and that we prioritise regeneration, infill and converting vacant homes before greenfield release to protect landscapes.

To increase affordable, good‑quality homes quickly, we need a mix of community‑led models and careful regeneration. I’d support reforms that enable community land trusts and housing co‑operatives to secure land at affordable terms, with public land allocated to them at low ground rent and a viability fund to bridge gaps so projects pencil. Expanding self‑build and using modern methods of construction (modular timber, off‑site fabrication) can cut build times, improve energy efficiency and quality, and give local people real alternatives. Local authorities also need streamlined planning support for small, community‑led sites and access to technical and procurement help to remove needless red tape.
Disagree: stricter licensing and longer tenancies could reduce supply by deterring investment; pilot rent caps carefully and protect small landlords while funding energy-efficient upgrades.

I strongly support reforms that would increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area by improving local data, strengthening monitoring, and boosting the planning and enforcement capacity of the council, while also raising energy standards for new builds and funding retrofits. Taken together, these measures would help ensure that commitments are actually delivered and that new housing is affordable to live in from day one.

First, we need a clear picture of what is being promised and what is being delivered. A live, publicly accessible housing delivery dashboard at the council level should track permissions granted, starts on site, completions, and the number and tenure mix of affordable units, with clear delivery milestones. It should also flag schemes where delivery is slipping and explain why. With this data, the council can intervene early, adjust conditions, or reallocate resources to schemes that are behind schedule. In my area, several large developments have touted 30–40% affordable housing on paper, but construction progress and unit delivery have lagged. A robust data framework would make those gaps transparent and drive accountability.

Second, make developers accountable for delivering affordable homes and ensure the council has the capacity to oversee delivery. This means stronger, enforceable planning conditions and predictable, timely viability checks. Where on‑site affordable housing isn’t feasible, cash‑in‑lieu or suitable off‑site provision should be offered, with a clear governance framework so funds are ring-fenced and spent on genuinely affordable homes in the same locality. It would help if planning performance agreements were the norm, with jointly agreed milestones and penalties for late delivery. To make this work, council planning teams—often overstretched—need extra funding and digital tools to manage complex mixed‑use schemes and post‑approval obligations.

Third, empower councils to deliver and enforce at pace. This includes funding to expand planning enforcement capacity, enable cross‑department collaboration (planning, housing, highways, and environmental teams), and invest in procurement and delivery capacity. When delivery obligations are not met, bonds or guarantees should be drawn, with funds redirected to accelerate new affordable homes elsewhere. In practice, this could look like an annual delivery plan for each big development, with quarterly reviews and explicit consequences for non‑delivery.

Fourth, raise energy standards for new homes and fund retrofits to protect tenants’ bills and meet climate targets. Mandating higher energy standards for all new builds—pursuing very high efficiency, low‑carbon heating, and well‑insulated, durable fabric—will reduce bills and improve living conditions from day one. Councils should be equipped to enforce these standards and to coordinate with energy suppliers and installers. At the same time, a council‑led retrofit programme should be funded to upgrade existing stock, including social housing and private rented properties. Grants or low‑interest loans for insulation, draughtproofing, heat pumps, and efficient boilers would cut energy bills for tenants and reduce carbon emissions. Where possible, retrofit schemes should be aligned with local job creation and apprenticeship opportunities, so improvements also support local skills.

In my neighbourhood, energy bills have risen sharply and the quality of some affordable homes is mixed—poor insulation and older, inefficient heating systems are common pain points. A combination of transparent delivery data, enforceable delivery duties for developers, and a strong retrofit fund would directly address these issues. It would also help ensure that new affordable homes are truly affordable in the long term, not just at the point of sale or completion.

To sum up, the reforms I back are practical and interconnected: better local data to illuminate the pipeline and enforce commitments; strengthened planning and enforcement capacity to ensure delivery; and ambitious energy standards for new homes coupled with a robust retrofit fund to improve existing stock. If implemented with clear targets and proper funding, these reforms would significantly increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes that people can actually afford to live in.

I’m writing as a pensioner living in England, watching the housing market from the vantage point of someone on a fixed income and who still cares deeply about our local towns and villages. I disagree with approaches that rely mainly on market-led bulk building with little regard to long‑term sustainability, amenity, or actual affordability for families and older people who need secure, good-quality homes. From my experience, the reforms that will truly increase supply in a way that works for communities are: purpose-built Build‑to‑Rent (BTR) and mixed‑tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management; funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or before housing; and careful use of rent stabilisation pilots to protect affordability without choking off investment.

Build‑to‑Rent and mixed-tenure schemes should be the cornerstone. Too often we see blocks of private flats built to sell, then kept empty or rented at eye‑watering rates because there’s no long‑term landlord stewardship. A properly designed BTR model, where a single operator manages a development over decades, changes the dynamic. It means reliable maintenance, predictable service levels, and a built‑in ethos of longevity rather than speculation. If a proportion of units in new schemes are covenanted to remain affordable (for example at a defined proportion of market rent, reviewed periodically), you create truly mixed communities rather than pockets of gentrification that push neighbours out of what should be a local, stable area.

In my town, I’ve watched a newer block with no affordability requirements become a luxury rental option that feels detached from the rest of the community. There’s no on-site management that understands concerns of older residents, and life becomes a constant search for somewhere else to live when repairs are slow or lifts break down. A BTR approach that comes with professional management, clear maintenance standards, and a built-in plan for accessibility features would have made that block part of the town rather than a floating asset for investors. Mixed tenure helps too — it protects social cohesion and keeps essential services within reach for everyone, not just those who can stretch to market rates.

But housing won’t stay affordable if services crawl along behind the houses. That’s why I advocate for funded, phased provision of transport, schools, GP services and utilities alongside or before housing. New communities must be service‑ready from day one. If a new estate ends up with a couple of extra buses and a temporary GP clinic a few years in, it won’t be fit for purpose for families or older residents who need quick access to healthcare and regular public transport. Planning conditions should require a credible, funded infrastructure plan that operates in step with housing delivery, not as an afterthought. In practice, that means tighter conditions on developers to co‑fund or front-load infrastructure and flexible, enforceable timelines for delivering those services.

On affordability, I welcome the idea of rent caps or stabilisation as a tool to guard against steep, sudden rises. However, I’m wary of applying caps without understanding the potential impact on supply. If rents are capped too tightly or for too long, experienced landlords may sell, invest elsewhere, or withdraw from management altogether, which reduces the stock and ultimately harms the very people we want to help. Pilots and evidence are essential. I’d support targeted, time‑bound rent caps in areas with acute affordability pressures, paired with robust monitoring of effects on maintenance, vacancy rates and new investment. The pilots should be transparent, with independent evaluation and a clear path to adjust policy based on what works.

In short, reforms that will genuinely boost supply are those that: (1) prioritise purpose-built Build‑to‑Rent with long‑term, professional management and affordability covenants; (2) insist on funded, phased infrastructure alongside housing so communities aren’t left with bricks and empty bus routes; and (3) test rent stabilisation carefully, with ongoing scrutiny about impacts on maintenance and new development. If we insist on short‑term stock numbers alone, we’ll merely replace one volatility with another—more flats, less quality, and a future where people like me worry about whether we can stay in our communities as costs rise.

I’m not against new homes. I’m asking for homes that are good for the long haul, that support healthy, connected lives for older residents and young families alike, and that don’t leave towns financially strapped or infrastructure-starved. The reforms described above are practical, evidence‑based, and more likely to deliver affordable, decent homes that endure.

Thank you for the chance to share my thoughts. I live in England and, like many households near towns with growing demand, I can see how the housing shortage affects affordability and quality. My instinct is to push for reforms that speed up planning and decision-making, but only if we keep strong environmental safeguards and a clear focus on high-quality, accessible homes. The experience in our area has shown that long, uncertain planning processes can lock in higher costs for developers and buyers alike, while delaying valuable amenities and infrastructure that new communities need.

What would help, in my view, is a balanced package that streamlines the process without undermining local character or biodiversity. Specific ideas include:

- Make planning timelines predictable and enforceable. Local authorities should publish firm milestones for plan preparation and for major and minor applications, with automatic extensions only in exceptional cases. A standardised pre-application route, with clear timescales, would help developers and communities alike. In practice, our borough has seen applications stall for months between consultation and decision, which pushes up costs and delays affordable delivery. A faster, predictable timetable would reduce developer uncertainty and help banks and builders plan more effectively.

- Simplify zoning with growth-focused designations while preserving safeguards. It would be helpful to have clear, locally tailored growth areas that allow infill and brownfield redevelopment near existing town centres and transport corridors, subject to strict environmental checks. This could accelerate delivery of affordable homes by removing needless steps for suitable sites, while still protecting green spaces, flood risk areas, and biodiversity. The key would be to attach robust tests for flood resilience, drainage, and climate adaptation at the same time as speeding approvals.

- Align affordable housing delivery with transparent viability tests. I would like to see clearer, more predictable obligations on affordable housing that don’t rely on repeated viability arguments that stall schemes. A reform could include standardised thresholds and a transparent appeal/monitoring process so that affordable units are delivered consistently and quickly. In our area, affordable homes sometimes reduce because financial viability is used as a reason to delay, which misses the point of providing genuinely affordable options for local people.

- Improve infrastructure funding and delivery linked to development. Speedy delivery must go hand in hand with timely provision of schools, GP surgeries, roads and public transport. A reform package could explore upfront funding for critical infrastructure via escrows or phased contributions linked to milestones, combined with clearer triggers for when infrastructure must be delivered.

- Prioritise quality, energy efficiency and accessibility. Streamlining should not mean lowering standards. New homes must be energy-efficient, well-insulated, and adaptable for older residents or changing needs. Reforms could include clearer national design and quality guidelines, supported by local design reviews that still allow communities to influence appearance and materials. This aligns with long-term affordability by reducing energy bills and maintenance costs.

- Support community-led and public-land initiatives. Public bodies and housing associations should be empowered to bring forward sites on public land, with simpler routes to consent and long-term stewardship. Community land trusts or co-housing models can help deliver mid-market and genuinely affordable homes if they’re given a clear, non-bureaucratic route to delivery.

In summary, I’m inclined to support reforms that accelerate housing delivery and reduce developer uncertainty, but only if we preserve rigorous environmental safeguards, high design quality, and fair, transparent mechanisms for affordable housing. If done well, these reforms could help us build more affordable, well-located homes without sacrificing the places we value. If not, there’s a real risk of hasty development that undermines flood resilience, green space, or community cohesion.

Thank you for considering these points.

Agree. Reforms should require funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or prior to housing to ensure sustainable, service-ready new communities. In practice, this means planning conditions and developer contributions must secure upfront or concurrent expansion of bus and rail connections, primary and secondary school places, GP capacity and essential utilities before homes are marketed. Without this, new developments strain already tight local services and undermine affordability through higher commuting costs and overcrowded facilities. Set clear, measurable targets: e.g., 100% of new homes connected to high-speed broadband, bus or rail timetables adjusted to new residents, and capacity in local clinics matching the pace of housing delivery within 0-2 years. Adopt infrastructure-first approvals: only grant outline consent if an agreed phased delivery plan is in place, supported by upfront levies or guarantees. Funding mechanisms should combine the Community Infrastructure Levy, Section 106 and government-backed infrastructure guarantees to share risk and accelerate delivery. Local experience in our area shows a large estate progressed with housing before a new school and GP capacity, leaving families waiting and long commutes. This approach would deliver genuinely affordable homes alongside thriving, sustainable communities.

Agree. In my area we need to prioritise regeneration, infill and conversions of vacant buildings and long term empty homes before touching greenfield land or releasing Green Belt. It protects landscapes and reduces car dependency by reusing sites close to existing services. A disused factory near my town centre has been idle for years; converting it to affordable flats would deliver homes quickly without sprawling new developments. I also back a requirement for funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or before housing to ensure new communities are sustainable. Without this, new families face overcrowded schools and stretched GP services, and commutes will grow. A policy that ties infrastructure upgrades to development, with clear milestones, would make sure services are ready when people move in. Practical steps I would support include streamlined planning rules for brownfield conversions; stronger incentives for bringing empty homes back into use; and ensuring quality standards, energy efficiency and accessible design. By fixing infrastructure first and reusing existing buildings, we can deliver affordable, high-quality homes while protecting our countryside.

I strongly support reforms that improve local data, monitoring, developer accountability and fund council planning, enforcement and delivery capacity to ensure commitments are delivered. In our town in Wales we have seen schemes approved with promised affordable components, but delivery lags because data on build-out rates and obligation tracking is weak and council delivery capacity is stretched. Strengthening local data on land supply, demand and vacancy would let councils set wiser targets and track progress more effectively, while clearer accountability would keep developers delivering planned affordable homes. Enhanced enforcement and ring-fenced funding for planning capacity would help us avoid long delays and substandard builds.

I also back targeted finance, procurement access, small-sites policy and planning support to help SME and local builders increase diverse, local housing supply. Small local builders often struggle to secure finance or win public contracts. A Welsh procurement framework that prioritises SMEs, plus dedicated finance facilities for small sites (5-15 homes), streamlined pre-application services and planning milestones, would unlock more sites and deliver better homes closer to towns and services. This combination would deliver more affordable, high-quality homes for Welsh communities.

From our organisation in England, simply releasing surplus public land and capturing uplift through levies or taxes is unlikely to deliver the affordable, good quality homes our area needs Obviously.... In practice land release can reduce competition and fail to prevent delays if planning and procurement are slow; uplift taxes create ongoing costs that can deter small builders and push up overall prices instead of reducing them. We have seen local parcels of public land sit unused for years while infrastructure and services struggle to keep up with demand; turning that land into housing requires careful time bound delivery and guaranteed ring fenced funding for infrastructure.

What would work better is a transparent local led approach: ensure affordable housing quotas on all viable schemes, with robust penalties for under delivery; support small and middle sized builders and community led housing to unlock small sites; accelerate planning with digital tools and single point of contact; commit long term funding for roads, schools and GP capacity tied to development; and apply value capture only where there is clear accountable delivery and measurable affordable housing outcomes. Without these safeguards lifting planning uplift and releasing land will not meaningfully increase supply or affordability.
